In its fiscal 2024 Form 10-K, Apple disclosed **four reported results** that were unfavorably affected by the weakness of foreign currencies against the U.S. dollar in the 2024 vs. 2023 comparison (all in Item 7, MD&A):

### 1–3. Segment net sales (three segments)

| Segment | 2024 vs. 2023 | Currency disclosure |
|---|---|---|
| **Greater China** | Net sales **decreased 8%** to $66,952M (primarily lower iPhone and iPad sales) | "**The weakness in the renminbi** relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Greater China net sales during 2024." |
| **Japan** | Net sales **increased 3%** to $25,052M (primarily higher iPhone sales) | "**The weakness in the yen** relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Japan net sales during 2024." |
| **Rest of Asia Pacific** | Net sales **increased 4%** to $30,658M (primarily higher Services sales) | "**The weakness in foreign currencies** relative to the U.S. dollar had a **net unfavorable** year-over-year impact on Rest of Asia Pacific net sales during 2024." |

The two **single named currencies** are the **renminbi** (Greater China) and the **yen** (Japan). Note that currency weakness was cited only as an *additional* headwind in these segments — the primary driver of the Greater China decline was lower iPhone and iPad sales, not currency.

### 4. Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage

"Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage increased during 2024 compared to 2023 due to cost savings, **partially offset by a different Products mix and the weakness in foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar**." (Products gross margin rose to $109,633M, 37.2% of sales, from $108,803M, 36.5%.)

### Not so affected (for contrast)
- **Americas** and **Europe** net sales are attributed solely to higher Services (and iPhone, in Europe) sales, with no currency impact cited.
- **Services gross margin** rose "due primarily to higher Services net sales," with no currency effect cited.
- **No currency effect** is cited for R&D, SG&A, the effective tax rate (24.1% vs. 14.7%, driven by the $10.2B State Aid Decision charge), or the value-at-risk statistic ($538M one-day loss vs. $669M in 2023).

### Supporting context (Item 7A, p. 27)
"Because the Company is a net receiver of currencies other than the U.S. dollar... a strengthening of the U.S. dollar will negatively affect the Company's net sales and gross margins as expressed in U.S. dollars." Apple may use derivatives, offset exposures, or adjust local pricing, but may leave certain exposures unhedged.

*Source: AAPL_2024_10K.pdf — MD&A "Segment Operating Performance" (p. 22 of the 10-K) and "Gross Margin" (p. 24), plus Item 7A and Item 1A risk factors.*

## 1. Item 1, Business — "Human Capital" (page 2 of the filing; PDF page 5)

Boeing states that as of December 31, 2023, its workforce included approximately 57,000 union members, and then gives a table with the column heading **"Union / Percent of our Employees Represented / Status of Major Agreements with Union"**:

| Union | Percent of employees represented | Major agreements |
|---|---|---|
| International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM) | **21%** | Two agreements: IAM District 751 (Washington) expiring Sept 2024; IAM District 837 (Missouri) expiring July 2025 |
| Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (SPEEA) | **10%** | Two agreements: SPEEA Professional and SPEEA Technical, both expiring Oct 2026 |
| United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW) | **1%** | One agreement: UAW District 1069 (Pennsylvania) expiring April 2027 |

## 2. Item 1A, Risk Factors — "Some of our and our suppliers' workforces are represented by labor unions, which may lead to work stoppages" (PDF page 12)

- **33%** — the aggregate: "Approximately 57,000 employees, which constitute 33% of our total workforce, were union represented as of December 31, 2023 under collective bargaining agreements with varying durations and expiration dates."

## Supporting context from the same filing
- Total workforce as of December 31, 2023: approximately **171,000** (vs. ~156,000 in 2022), with 14% located outside the U.S.
- Boeing maintains union relationships with **10 U.S. labor organizations and 4 non-U.S. labor organizations**.
- The risk factor notes Boeing experienced a work stoppage in 2008 when a labor strike halted commercial aircraft and certain BDS program production.

**Note on the arithmetic:** 21% + 10% + 1% = 32%, which approximates the 33% aggregate figure (the slight gap reflects the table being based on rounded percentages and on the three largest unions only, while the 57,000/33% figure includes all 14 labor organizations).

## Boeing 2025 Form 10-K (BA_2025_10K.pdf) — IAM District 837 disclosures

### 1. The 2025 strike by IAM District 837 employees

| Item | What the filing says |
|---|---|
| Employees | "approximately 3,200 employees at our St. Louis area sites" |
| Duration | **101 days** |
| Start date | Work stoppage **initiated August 4, 2025** |
| End date | Ended when IAM 837 voted to ratify a new contract on **November 13, 2025** |
| Impact | Disrupted Boeing's St. Louis operations; impacted programs including **F/A-18, F-15, T-7A Red Hawk, MQ-25 and Weapons** |

**What it refers to:** the work stoppage itself — the number of employees in the struck bargaining unit, how long the stoppage lasted, and the calendar window during which it occurred. It is not a contract term.

**Where it appears:** Item 1 Business — Human Capital (p. 4); Item 1A Risk Factors (pp. 11–12); and Item 7 MD&A — Overview (p. 26).

### 2. The current collective bargaining agreement with IAM District 837

| Item | What the filing says |
|---|---|
| Union | The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM) — **25% of total workforce** |
| Agreement | **IAM District 837** |
| Principal location | **Missouri** (St. Louis area) |
| Expiration date | **July 2030** |

**What it refers to:** the expiration date of the collective bargaining agreement currently in force with District 837 — i.e., the successor contract ratified on November 13, 2025 that ended the strike. The filing gives the expiration month/year only; it does not state a contract term length in years or a start date for the agreement itself.

**Where it appears:** the "principal collective bargaining agreements" table in Item 1 — Human Capital (p. 4).

### Distinctions worth noting

- **101 days vs. 53 days:** the 101-day figure is the 2025 IAM 837 stoppage. Do not conflate it with the **2024 IAM District 751 strike** (over 30,000 manufacturing employees, primarily Washington state; initiated September 13, 2024, ended by ratification on November 4, 2024; **53 days**), which the filing lists separately and which is the one that halted most commercial aircraft production.
- **Strike dates vs. agreement dates:** August 4 – November 13, 2025 describes the *stoppage*; July 2030 describes the *expiration of the current agreement* that replaced the contract under which the strike occurred.
- **Tentative agreement ≠ ratified contract:** the filing notes that both the IAM 751 and IAM 837 strikes occurred even though union leadership had reached a tentative agreement and recommended ratification — hence the 101-day figure reflects the full time members were out, not the time until the tentative agreement.
- **Other expiries nearby:** Boeing separately flags SPEEA contracts (about 16,000 employees) expiring in **October 2026**, and the Human Capital table lists IAM District 70 (Kansas, June 2027) and District 751 (Washington, September 2028) among its principal agreements.
- **Aggregate context:** as of December 31, 2025, Boeing's total workforce was approximately 182,000, of which about 72,000 (40%) were union-represented under 32 independent U.S. agreements with nine unions, plus agreements with 18 international representative bodies.

I reviewed Apple's fiscal 2025 Form 10-K (`AAPL_2025_10K.pdf`, fiscal year ended September 27, 2025). The filing dates developments to a specific day or month of calendar 2025 in four places.

## The dated 2025 developments

**April 23, 2025 — EU Commission DMA decisions (two actions, same day)** (Item 3, Legal Proceedings, p. 18 of the 10-K)
- In the **Article 5(4) Investigation** (opened March 25, 2024, regarding how developers may communicate/promote offers and conclude contracts with end users), the Commission **fined Apple €500 million and issued a cease and desist order** requiring Apple to remove technical and commercial restrictions preventing developers from steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store. Apple has appealed this decision.
- **Also on April 23, 2025**, the Commission **issued preliminary findings** in the **Article 6(4) Investigation** (opened June 24, 2024, concerning Apple's new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces). If the Commission makes a final violation determination, it can issue a cease and desist order and may impose fines **up to 10% of Apple's annual worldwide net sales**.

**April 30, 2025 — Epic Games ruling (California District Court)** (Item 3)
- The court **found Apple in violation of the 2021 Injunction** and enjoined Apple from imposing any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app; from restricting, conditioning, limiting, or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to purchases outside an app; or otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of an app.
- The court also **denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction** and **referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate**. Apple appealed to the Ninth Circuit.

**September 2, 2025 — Google search remedies (D.C. District Court)** (Risk Factors, p. 14) — a matter involving a company with which Apple has a commercial relationship (Apple's Google search licensing arrangements). Following Google's August 5, 2024 antitrust violation finding, the D.C. District Court **ordered certain remedies**. The order is subject to further proceedings before that court (which may change the interpretation or application of the remedies, or order new or changed remedies) and to **appeal by both the DOJ and Google**. A reversal on appeal could impose remedies the DOJ initially proposed, such as prohibiting Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution, which could materially affect Apple's search licensing revenue.

**October 2025 — Ninth Circuit oral argument (Epic Games)** (Item 3) — although Apple's request to stay the decision pending appeal was denied, the Ninth Circuit agreed to hear Apple's appeal on an **expedited basis, with oral arguments heard in October 2025**.

## Related but not day/month-specific
- **Fourth quarter of 2025**: Apple settled certain ordinary-course legal matters that "did not individually or in the aggregate have a material impact" on financial condition or operating results (Item 3; Note 12 Contingencies also states no reasonable possibility of a material loss beyond recorded accruals).
- **Beginning in the second quarter of 2025**: new U.S. tariffs and reciprocal retaliatory measures were announced, and Commerce initiated a **Section 232** investigation into semiconductor imports (MD&A, p. 22) — dated only to a quarter, not a day or month.

Notably, the **DOJ antitrust lawsuit** (filed March 21, 2024 in the District of New Jersey) and the DOJ/state private antitrust suits received **no 2025-dated developments** in this filing.

## NVIDIA FY2024 Form 10-K (FY ended January 28, 2024) — Inventory-related charges to cost of revenue

### 1. Combined total provision: $2.2 billion
MD&A, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin" (p. 40):
> "Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled $2.2 billion for both fiscal years 2024 and 2023."

This $2.2 billion is the combined fiscal 2024 charge to cost of revenue for (a) excess/obsolete inventory write-downs and (b) excess inventory purchase obligations. The two components are quantified separately in Note 10 and add up to this total.

### 2. Component: $774 million — inventory (excess/obsolete) provision
Note 10, Balance Sheet Components, footnote to Inventories (p. 68):
> "In fiscal years 2024 and 2023, we recorded an inventory provision of $774 million and $1.0 billion, respectively, in cost of revenue."

Represents the write-down of inventory on the balance sheet to the lower of cost or net realizable value for obsolete or excess inventory. Per Note 1 (p. 58), most of these provisions "relate to excess quantities of products, based on our inventory levels and future product purchase commitments compared to assumptions about future demand and market conditions."

### 3. Component: ~$1.4 billion — excess inventory purchase obligation expense
Note 10, footnote to "Accrued and Other Current Liabilities" (p. 70):
> "In fiscal years 2024 and 2023, we recorded an expense of approximately $1.4 billion and $1.1 billion, respectively, in cost of revenue for inventory purchase obligations in excess of our current demand projections, supplier charges and for penalties related to cancellations and underutilization."

Represents non-cancellable supplier purchase commitments for quantities exceeding NVIDIA's demand forecasts, plus related supplier charges and cancellation/underutilization penalties. Note 1 explains NVIDIA "record[s] a liability for noncancelable purchase commitments with suppliers for quantities in excess of our future demand forecasts."

Note: $774 million + ~$1.4 billion ≈ $2.2 billion, reconciling the Note 10 components to the MD&A combined total.

### 4. Provision release (credit to cost of revenue): $540 million
MD&A, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin" (p. 40):
> "Sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations resulted in a provision release of $540 million and $137 million for fiscal years 2024 and 2023, respectively."

This is the fiscal 2024 release, arising from selling inventory already written down and from settling excess inventory purchase obligations. The filing does not split the $540 million between the inventory and purchase-obligation components, nor does it state the net charge directly. (Note 1 confirms that written-down inventory establishes a new cost basis that "is not subsequently written up," so the release comes from disposal of reserved items and settlement of obligations, not from write-ups.)

### 5. Implied net amount (derived, not a stated filing figure)
$2.2 billion gross provisions less $540 million release = approximately **$1.66 billion net charge** to cost of revenue in fiscal 2024 for these items. NVIDIA does not present this net figure directly in the filing.

### Corroborating disclosure (no dollar amounts)
PwC's critical audit matter, "Valuation of Inventories – Provisions for Excess or Obsolete Inventories and Excess Product Purchase Commitments" (p. 49), confirms the nature of these charges — "the Company charges cost of sales for inventory provisions to write-down inventory for excess or obsolete inventory and for excess product purchase commitments" — and cites Notes 1, 10 and 13. It cites only balance-sheet amounts, which are excluded per your instructions.

### Excluded per your instructions
- Excess inventory purchase obligations balance outstanding at year-end ($1,655 million) and the $5,282 million total inventories balance.
- The $16.1 billion outstanding inventory purchase and long-term supply/capacity obligations, and $20,707 million total future purchase commitments (Note 13).
- Percentage impacts on gross margin (the 2.7% unfavorable net effect in fiscal 2024).
- All fiscal 2023 amounts ($1.0 billion inventory provision, ~$1.1 billion purchase-obligation expense, $137 million release).

JPMorgan Chase adopted **FASB ASU 2022-02, "Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings and Vintage Disclosures"**, on **January 1, 2023**, under the **modified retrospective method**. The 10-K reports the adoption effect in three places:

### 1. Allowance for credit losses (allowance for loan losses): net decrease of **$587 million**

| Portfolio segment | Cumulative effect of change in accounting principle (Jan 1, 2023) |
|---|---|
| Consumer, excluding credit card | $(489) million |
| Credit card | $(100) million |
| Wholesale | $2 million |
| **Total (Firm)** | **$(587) million** |

*Source: Note 13, "Allowance for credit losses and related information" table (10-K p. 258); also described in Note 13 text (p. 256) and in MD&A "Allowance for credit losses" (p. 131): "The allowance for credit losses also reflected a reduction of $587 million as a result of the adoption of changes to the TDR accounting guidance on January 1, 2023."*

**What it measures:** The pretax reduction in the Firm's estimate of expected credit losses on its retained (held-for-investment) loan portfolios. Because the new guidance eliminated TDR accounting and the requirement to measure the allowance on TDRs using a discounted cash flow (DCF) method, the Firm elected a non‑DCF, portfolio‑based allowance approach for loans modified for borrowers experiencing financial difficulty (all portfolios except collateral‑dependent loans and nonaccrual risk‑rated loans, which remain asset‑specific/DCF). The $587 million is a contra‑asset reduction in the allowance (a credit valuation account) recorded as an opening adjustment at January 1, 2023 — it is *not* a 2023 provision. It was "predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card." There was no impact on the allowance for lending‑related commitments (shown as "NA") or on the allowance for credit losses on investment securities.

### 2. Retained earnings: increase of **$446 million, after tax**

*Source: Note 1, "Accounting standards adopted January 1, 2023" (10-K p. 173), repeated in Note 13 (p. 256).*

**What it measures:** The after‑tax opening adjustment to shareholders' equity resulting from the same modified retrospective adoption — i.e., the pretax $587 million allowance release net of the related deferred tax effect (an implied tax effect of roughly $141 million). It is a permanent increase to capital/retained earnings, not a 2023 earnings item; the effect is also stated to be predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card.

### Related context (equity statement)

The Consolidated statements of changes in stockholders' equity show a 2023 line, **"Cumulative effect of change in accounting principles: $449 million"** (10-K p. 169). This is the **combined** opening adjustment for *both* standards adopted on January 1, 2023 — the TDR guidance ($446 million) and the Derivatives and Hedging: Fair Value Hedging – Portfolio Layer Method (the HTM‑to‑AFS transfer election, whose retained‑earnings impact Note 1 states "was not material," accounting for the roughly $3 million difference).

### What the change did in substance

- Eliminated TDR accounting and disclosure (including the "reasonably expected"/"concession" assessment) and the mandatory DCF allowance measurement for TDRs; if DCF is still applied, the discount rate must now be the post‑modification effective interest rate.
- Replaced TDR disclosures with disclosures of modifications for borrowers experiencing financial difficulty ("FDMs"), plus current‑period gross charge‑offs by origination vintage.
- As a result, the population of FDM loans is larger than the population previously classified as TDRs (e.g., 2023 consumer FDM volume of $136 million in residential real estate and $648 million in credit card versus 2022 new TDR balances of $418 million in credit card and $801 million in wholesale).

I found the relevant disclosures in Boeing's 2022 Form 10-K (`BA_2022_10K.pdf`). Here are the fixed-price contract percentages for 2022 revenue:

## Percentages of 2022 revenue on fixed-price contracts

| Percentage | Applies to | Where stated |
|---|---|---|
| **100%** | Commercial Airplanes (BCA) | Note 22 – Segment and Revenue Information (PDF p. 111 / 10-K p. 109): "Revenue recognized on fixed-price contracts 100 %" |
| **60%** | Defense, Space & Security (BDS) | Note 22 (PDF p. 111): "Revenue recognized on fixed-price contracts 60 %" (vs. 68% in 2021, 69% in 2020) |
| **88%** | Global Services (BGS) — total segment | Note 22 (PDF p. 112): "Revenue recognized on fixed-price contracts 88 %" (vs. 86% in 2021, 87% in 2020) |

## Important nuance on the BGS figure

Item 1A Risk Factors ("We enter into fixed-price contracts which could subject us to losses if we have cost overruns," PDF p. 15 / 10-K p. 13) states a *different* pair of percentages:

> "Our **BDS and BGS defense businesses** generated approximately **60% and 69%** of their 2022 revenues from fixed-price contracts."

So the filing offers two BGS-related percentages that are not the same measure:
- **88%** = fixed-price share of the **entire BGS segment** (Note 22)
- **69%** = fixed-price share of the **BGS defense/government-services business only** (Risk Factors)

The complementary cost-type disclosure in the same risk factor says BDS and the BGS defense business generated approximately **40%** and **31%** of 2022 revenues from cost-type contracting arrangements (100% − 60% = 40% for BDS).

## Other relevant context

- Boeing Capital (BCC) has **no fixed-price percentage disclosed** — its $199 million of 2022 revenue is lease interest income and related items, not contract revenue.
- For contrast, the filing separately states that **40%** of consolidated 2022 revenue was earned pursuant to U.S. government contracts (Note 22 and Risk Factors, PDF p. 14) — a different metric, not fixed-price revenue.
- Related fixed-price exposure disclosure: BDS recorded 2022 charges on fixed-price development programs including VC-25B ($1,452M), KC-46A Tanker ($1,374M), MQ-25 ($579M), T-7A Red Hawk Production Options ($552M), T-7A Red Hawk EMD ($203M), and Commercial Crew ($288M).

## NVIDIA FY2026 Form 10-K — Goodwill Amounts

### 1. Balance at January 25, 2026

**Total goodwill: $20.8 billion ($20,832 million on the balance sheet)** — Note 5, page 63

| Reporting unit | Goodwill at Jan 25, 2026 |
|---|---|
| Compute & Networking | $20.5 billion |
| Graphics | $370 million |
| **Total** | **$20.8 billion ($20,832M)** |

The $370 million Graphics balance is unchanged from the prior year (it is inherited legacy goodwill, not a fiscal 2026 addition). No goodwill impairment was recognized; annual qualitative impairment tests in Q4 of fiscal 2026, 2025, and 2024 all concluded goodwill was not impaired.

### 2. Goodwill added during fiscal 2026

**$15.6 billion increase in goodwill, all allocated to the Compute & Networking reporting unit** (Note 5; $20,832M − $5,188M = $15,644M).

The principal driver, and the only transaction with a separately disclosed goodwill component, is the **Groq transaction (Note 2, page 61)**:

- **$14.4 billion of goodwill** recorded in December 2025 from the non-exclusive license of Groq, Inc.'s language processing unit (LPU) technology plus the hiring of certain Groq employees. No customer contracts, existing products, or equity interests were purchased.
  - The goodwill is **primarily attributable to the acquired workforce and the future development of the licensed technology**.
  - It was recorded in the **Compute & Networking** reporting unit and is **tax deductible**.
  - The associated $2.5 billion developed-technology intangible asset was valued using a **cost-to-recreate methodology** with a five-year useful life.
  - Consideration: **$13.0 billion paid at closing** plus **$4 billion (inclusive of imputed interest) payable within one year**, recorded in Accrued and Other Current Liabilities. Pro forma results were omitted as the effect was not material.

**Derived (not separately disclosed):** the remaining ~$1.2 billion of the $15.6 billion increase is not attributed to a named transaction in the filing. It most plausibly reflects the other acquisitions shown as "Acquisitions, net of cash acquired" of $1,535 million in fiscal 2026 investing activities (Note 1's business-combination policy allows up to one year of measurement-period adjustments offset to goodwill), but the 10-K does not break this out. Flagging this as inference, not a disclosed figure.

### Other context
- Goodwill is allocated to reporting units based on expected benefit from the business combination, and is tested annually in Q4 (or earlier on impairment indicators).
- Segment long-lived-asset disclosures (Note 16) explicitly exclude goodwill and intangible assets.
- On December 15, 2025 NVIDIA acquired a company and issued 174,676 shares (~$31 million) to a key employee; the $28 million of "fair value of partially vested equity awards assumed in connection with acquisitions" in the equity statement is APIC, not goodwill.

**Bottom line:** $20.8 billion total goodwill at January 25, 2026 ($20.5B Compute & Networking + $370M Graphics), of which $15.6 billion was added in fiscal 2026 — chiefly the $14.4 billion of tax-deductible Groq goodwill for the acquired workforce and future licensed-technology development, plus ~$1.2 billion from other/undisclosed acquisitions and measurement-period adjustments.

## Pfizer 2021 Form 10-K — Upjohn separation costs

The filing quantifies these costs in two places: MD&A (forward-looking total) and Note 2B "Divestitures" (amounts actually incurred). Here are the figures exactly as the filing states them.

### 1. MD&A — "Our Business and Strategy" (10-K p. 26)
> "We expect to incur costs of **approximately $700 million** in connection with separating Upjohn, of which, **approximately 75%** has been incurred since inception and through December 31, 2021. These charges include costs and expenses related to **separation of legal entities** and **transaction costs**."

This is the forward-looking total expected cost of the separation, with the 75%-incurred figure measured from inception through December 31, 2021.

### 2. Note 2B — "Upjohn Separation and Combination with Mylan" (10-K p. 65)
> "As a result of the separation of Upjohn, we incurred **separation-related costs of $434 million in 2020** and **$83 million in 2019**, which are included in *Discontinued operations–net of tax*. These costs primarily relate to **professional fees for regulatory filings** and **separation activities within finance, tax, legal and information system functions** as well as **investment banking fees**."

| Figure | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **$434 million (2020)** | Separation-related costs incurred in 2020, recorded within Discontinued operations–net of tax |
| **$83 million (2019)** | Separation-related costs incurred in 2019, recorded within Discontinued operations–net of tax |
| **Approximately $700 million** | Total expected costs in connection with separating Upjohn; approximately 75% incurred from inception through December 31, 2021; comprises separation of legal entities and transaction costs |

Note the internal consistency: $434 million + $83 million = $517 million, which is approximately 75% of the $700 million expected total, reconciling the two disclosures.

### Related separation items that are *not* separation costs
For clarity, the filing also discloses several Upjohn-related amounts that are separate from the cost figures above:

2. **Reduced aircraft production levels**, which "reflected order delays and cancellations by airlines and inventory reduction initiatives within the industry" — in both 2021 and 2020.

The Item 1 business description expands on this and is the most explicit statement in the filing:

So the filing identifies four compounding factors:

- **Sharp, sudden reductions in air travel** (both domestic and international), which drove down aircraft build rates.
- **Unprecedented customer destocking** — the filing describes it as occurring "at extraordinary rates."
- **Airline order delays and cancellations**, and industry-wide inventory-reduction initiatives, which depressed OEM production and hence PCC's shipments.
- **Boeing 737 MAX and 787 program production delays**, which the filing says "adversely impacted PCC over the past three years" (i.e., spanning 2020–2022). Berkshire's 2024 Form 10-K gives two explicit reasons for evaluating BHE on an after‑tax basis, and the surrounding disclosures show why those reasons matter.

**1. It reflects how the energy businesses are actually managed and evaluated (MD&A).**

In the BHE section of Management's Discussion and Analysis, the filing states: *"The discussion of BHE's operating results that follows is based on after-tax earnings, reflecting how the energy businesses are managed and evaluated."* (page K‑43). So after-tax earnings is the measure BHE's own management uses internally, and Berkshire presents it that way in the MD&A segment tables (U.S. utilities, natural gas pipelines, other energy businesses, real estate brokerage, corporate interest and other — all on a net earnings basis).

**2. Income taxes are a material driver of BHE's economics because of production tax credits and the related regulatory effects (Note 26, Business segment data).**

The segment note directly contrasts BHE with Berkshire's other non-insurance businesses: *"For most non-insurance businesses, pre-tax earnings are considered in allocating resources and capital, although income taxes are also considered at BHE, given the magnitude of production tax credits associated with wind-powered electricity generation investments and the related impacts from regulation."* (page K‑109).

The magnitude is extreme: BHE's income tax line is a **benefit**, not an expense — $1,871 million in 2024, $2,022 million in 2023 and $1,629 million in 2022 — producing **negative effective income tax rates of (81.6)%, (215.1)% and (51.8)%**, respectively, with the footnote noting these amounts *"include significant production tax credits primarily from wind-powered electricity generation"* (page K‑43). On top of that, U.S. income tax credits at the consolidated level *"derive primarily from production tax credits associated with wind-energy generation of BHE"* (Note 20). With taxes exceeding pretax earnings, pretax earnings would bear little relationship to BHE's actual economic result, so management must look at after-tax figures.

**Supporting context in the filing.**

- *Rate-setting makes taxes a cost of the business.* BHE's regulated businesses set rates *"largely based on the costs of business operations, including income taxes and a return on capital, and are subject to regulatory approval,"* and to the extent such costs are not allowed in approved rates, *"operating results will be adversely affected"* (page K‑43). State commissions set cost-of-service rates that allow recovery of reasonable costs *"including the opportunity to earn a fair and reasonable return on its investments"* (page K‑9). The earnings that matter to BHE are therefore inherently after-tax.
- *Taxes also drive the year-over-year comparisons discussed in the MD&A*, including the U.K. Energy Profits Levy and deferred income tax expense at Northern Powergrid, a group relief tax benefit in 2024, the higher effective income tax rate at the natural gas pipelines following the September 2023 purchase of an additional 50% of Cove Point, and the loss of wind tax-equity investment earnings (pages K‑44–K‑45). BHE's large third-party wind tax-equity investment program (about $7.3 billion) means tax benefits are a core earnings driver.
- *Wildfire accruals and other items are also presented after tax*, and the filing notes that BHE's "corporate interest and other" line is an after-tax measure that includes unallocated corporate income tax expenses.

In short, the filing says BHE is discussed after tax simply because that is how the energy businesses are managed and evaluated, and because income taxes — dominated by wind production tax credits and inseparable from the regulated cost-of-service rate-setting process — are too large and too consequential for pretax earnings to be an adequate yardstick at BHE.
